results.title: NVIDIA A100, H100, and B200 Rental Prices Rise as AI Demand Stays Strong
highlights:
Rental prices for several generations of NVIDIA data centre GPUs have continued to increase during 2026, challenging the idea that older AI accelerators quickly lose their commercial value when newer hardware arrives.

Market data cited in the report shows that hourly rental rates for the H100 have moved above $2 and are approaching $3, compared with just under $2 at the start of the year. The newer B200 has also increased from slightly below $5 per hour in January to roughly $5.50 to $5.80.

Older models, including the A100, are reportedly seeing stronger pricing as well. The trend suggests that demand for AI computing remains high enough to support multiple generations of hardware rather than shifting entirely toward the latest processors.

This does not prove that AI infrastructure is free from overinvestment risks. However, rising rental prices indicate that available GPU capacity is still valuable across cloud platforms and specialised compute providers.

...

The B200 currently commands the highest hourly price among the GPUs discussed, while the H100 remains widely used for model training and inference.

| NVIDIA GPU | Approximate January 2026 rate | Recent reported rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | Just under $2 per hour | Above $2 and approaching $3 |
| B200 | Just under $5 per hour | Around $5.50 to $5.80 |
| A100 | Not specified | Reportedly increasing |
| H200 | Not specified | Reportedly increasing |

The available figures come from rental market data rather than NVIDIA’s official selling prices. Rates can vary based on the provider, contract length, region, networking, storage, software environment, and whether the GPU is rented individually or as part of a larger cluster.

Spot rental prices can also change quickly when supply is limited or customers need hardware immediately.

...

When AI inference becomes cheaper, companies may use more of it. Developers can add AI features to more applications, serve more customers, run larger context windows, and increase the number of automated tasks.

This creates a situation where lower cost per token leads to higher overall consumption of computing resources.

...

## High rental rates do not remove every risk

Strong pricing may reflect genuine demand, but it can also be influenced by short term shortages.

The supply of complete AI systems depends on more than GPU chips. High bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, networking equipment, cooling systems, power availability, and data centre construction can all limit capacity.

| Market risk | Possible impact |
| --- | --- |
| New GPU supply increases | Rental prices could decline |
| Competing accelerators improve | NVIDIA hardware may lose pricing power |
| AI demand slows | Utilisation and rental rates could fall |
| Electricity costs rise | Older GPUs may become less economical |
| Software shifts | Some workloads may move to specialised chips |
| Excess data centre construction | Available capacity could exceed demand |

Older GPUs can also consume more power per unit of work than newer models. Even if their hourly rental price remains high, operating margins may be lower once electricity and cooling costs are included.

The latest rental data therefore supports a longer useful life argument, but it does not settle the debate.

...

The B200’s reported rate of approximately $5.50 to $5.80 per hour shows that customers are willing to pay a substantial premium for the latest available performance.

Newer GPUs can complete work faster, support larger models, and provide more memory or stronger interconnect capabilities. That can make them cheaper on a per task basis even when the hourly rate is higher.

A customer training a large model may prefer the B200 if it shortens the total completion time enough to offset the higher rental cost.

At the same time, H100 and A100 systems can remain more economical for workloads that do not need the newest architecture.

The rising prices across several generations show that the market is not treating AI GPUs as immediately obsolete assets. Older NVIDIA accelerators continue to generate revenue, while the B200 commands a premium near $6 per hour.

How long this trend lasts will depend on future supply, AI adoption, electricity costs, software efficiency, and the arrival of competing hardware. For now, the rental market suggests that demand remains strong enough to support both current and previous generations of NVIDIA data centre GPUs.

results.title: This chart is one of the strongest arguments for why neoclouds are positioned to print money. | Rui Zhang 张芮, CFA
highlights:
SpaceX is generating $30–50 million in annualized revenue per active megawatt of compute.

Pure-play neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN) sit at $9.4–10.4 million per MW.
Traditional colocation players (Digital Realty, Equinix) lag at just $3.5–4.4 million.

That gap is the opportunity.

The mechanism that closes it is rising GPU rental pricing — the opposite of what most people expect in a “commoditized” market.

• One-year H100 rates jumped ~40%, from $1.70/GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.60 today.
• On-demand is effectively sold out. Blackwell B200 pricing runs $4.99–$18 per hour.
• Providers are raising, not cutting, published rates (Lambda $2.99 → $4.29; Verda $2.29 → $3.25).

This creates a self-reinforcing cycle: tighter supply → higher prices → more hardware locked in → even tighter supply.

Power and megawatts are the scarce fixed input. GPU lead times already stretch 36–52 weeks, and Gartner expects power constraints to limit 40% of AI data centers by 2027.

If a neocloud already has power secured and GPUs deployed, rising per-GPU-hour rates flow almost directly into higher revenue per megawatt — with minimal incremental capex.

That is why CoreWeave, Nebius and peers sit so far above legacy colocation on this chart.
Colocation rents space and power.

Neoclouds capture the pricing power of the actual compute running on top of it.

As GPU scarcity persists, that spread should keep widening.

results.title: Mark Zuckerberg Says Buyers Are Offering Meta a 'Significant Premium' for Its Compute — But He Turned Them Down, Calls Selling 'Foolish'
highlights:
Mark Zuckerberg recently told investors that other companies are trying to buy Meta Platforms' (META) computing power at a markup — and that he intends to keep most of it anyway.

The subject came up on Meta's second-quarter earnings call on July 29, when an analyst asked how the company thinks about the offers it is fielding to sell compute while it is buying compute itself. The CEO started with the market condition. "The high-level observation is that there's just nowhere near enough compute for all the demand," he said. "That is why we see that basically we are getting a large number of offers for the compute that we have."

In his prepared remarks, Zuckerberg had already put a price on it: "We're getting a lot of offers for compute at a significant premium over what we paid for it."

...

The CEO explained why the answer is mostly no. “It would be foolish to basically just sell all of the compute and take a short-term profit […] when you have the opportunity to build intelligence on top of it, which will be a multiple […] that compounds the value of the compute on top of that,” he said.

...

“You don't want to only do long-term things and not kind of prove the markets out that exist in the near term,” Zuckerberg noted, while also saying that Meta wants "the ability to monetize the compute directly when that makes sense," alongside the intelligence built on top of it.

The commercial ambition is broader than reselling capacity. Zuckerberg listed a third leg of the business alongside the apps and the agents. “We see a large enterprise opportunity to sell to businesses, including APIs, business agents, potentially selling compute directly, and other services that we're building for large customers.” He also described where the pricing model ends up. "Over time, that will let us run an efficient auction over our compute, similar to how we do that for our advertisers today," the CEO said. An auction over compute is a fair description of a cloud business.

Meta is building the capacity to have that problem. Zuckerberg noted that, the day before the earnings call, Meta announced a venture with BlackRock (BLK) to develop a 1 gigawatt data center in El Paso, Texas, as part of what the company calls its Meta Compute effort. He said the company continues to "invest aggressively in infrastructure to meet the demand."

...

"There is a lead time where we're investing in building out these data centers now," Zuckerberg said. ... You obviously are not getting value out of them until they're online."

results.title: Medium
highlights:
The memory market in 2026 is in its most severe shortage in ~15 years. HBM is sold out through 2026 across SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron; DRAM prices surged ~90% in Q1 2026 alone, and per a July 2026 Bloomberg report cited widely, DRAM spot prices had climbed nearly 700% over the trailing year (a June 2026 Sherman Act class action against the three makers alleges a comparable ~700% consumer price rise over four years); contract DDR5 more than doubled; SK hynix posted a 72% operating margin and Micron’s net profit surged ~770% year-on-year. HBM4 is priced 60–70% above HBM3E — per Korea Economic Daily/BusinessKorea reporting (via TrendForce), SK hynix’s 12-Hi HBM4 to Nvidia is priced at ~$500, “60%-70% higher than the HBM3E of the same specification (about US$300),” with per-Gb pricing forecast to rise from ~$2 in H2 2026 to $4–5+ in 2027. Micron notes a ~3:1 wafer-conversion ratio — every HBM gigabyte consumes ~3x the wafer capacity of standard DRAM — which is why the shortage bled into consumer DRAM and NAND.

Efficiency versus Jevons — my explicit model and verdict. The user asks whether MLA, sparse attention, quantization, tiered storage, and better batching reduce aggregate HBM demand per unit of served intelligence. Per unit, unambiguously yes — MLA cuts KV bytes 2.7–64x, MoE cuts active-parameter reads, FP4 halves weight bytes versus FP8. But aggregate demand is (intelligence served) × (HBM per unit), and the first term is exploding faster than the second is shrinking. Reasoning models emit 10–100x more tokens per task; agents multiply calls; video/multimodal is far more memory-hungry than text. SemiAnalysis explicitly rejects the efficiency-reduces-demand thesis, invoking Jevons: cheaper inference widens adoption, and even efficient trillion-parameter models like Kimi K3 need >1.5TB HBM for weights alone, forcing KV offload and requiring 64+-chip NVLink scale-up domains. My verdict: through 2027, Jevons dominates decisively — aggregate HBM demand keeps rising, and the shortage is more likely under-estimated than over-estimated near-term. The efficiency techniques change where memory demand lands (more capacity tiers, relatively less pure-HBM per token) but not the direction of aggregate demand. The genuine risk — flagged by TrendForce as a possible post-2026 correction — is a supply-driven glut in 2027–2028 as capacity expansions land and Chinese domestic HBM catches up, not a demand collapse from efficiency.

Leading indicators to watch . You should monitor: (1) hyperscaler capex guidance revisions — the ~$725B combined 2026 figure (Microsoft ~$190B, Amazon ~$200B, Google $175–205B, Meta $115–145B, with Microsoft’s CFO attributing ~$25B of the figure to rising memory-chip and component costs) and whether 2027 exceeds the projected $1T; a downward revision is the first sign of demand deceleration. (2) HBM4 qualification and pricing — if the 60–70% premium erodes fast, supply is catching up. (3) Memory-maker capacity conversions back toward standard DRAM. (4) Token-price deflation rate — acceleration signals oversupply of compute. (5) Inference-provider utilization and margin. (6) H100 hourly spot rental rates — a sustained fall signals slack. (7) Emergence of prefill-optimized silicon (Rubin CPX) and inference ASICs shifting the prefill:decode traffic ratio. (8) CXL/HBF adoption milestones (HBF samples H2 2026, products early 2027). (9) The prefill:decode traffic ratio itself as agents proliferate — more prefill-heavy (long-context, high-cache-hit) traffic favors flash tiers over HBM.

Has the bottleneck migrated? Yes — decisively to power. GPU supply eased after 2023 as TSMC roughly doubled CoWoS capacity multiple times. The binding constraint in 2026 is electrical: high-voltage transformer lead times stretched from 24–30 months pre-2020 to 3–5 years (Wood Mackenzie’s 2025 survey put power transformers at ~128 weeks and generator step-ups at ~144 weeks); medium-voltage switchgear is effectively sold out through 2028; grid interconnection queues span years (only 13% of 2000–2019 interconnection requests reached operation by end-2024); and an estimated 30–50% of planned 2026 US datacenter openings will be delayed or cancelled, with only ~5 GW under construction of ~16 GW announced. Electrical equipment is <10% of datacenter cost but 100% of the bottleneck. SemiAnalysis projects Anthropic+OpenAI unconstrained compute demand exceeding 100 GW by 2030 against net additions of only 2.5 GW (2025) and 5 GW (2026). The new currency is power-per-token, and the new hardware trend is prefill/decode-disaggregated silicon (Rubin CPX, the reported Groq LPU decode partnership), inference ASICs (Groq, Cerebras, Etched, d-Matrix, Positron, Tenstorrent), scale-up NVLink/UALink domains, co-packaged optics, and FP4/NVFP4/MXFP4 as the standard inference precision. CPU/substrate/ABF and CoWoS packaging are secondary tight points; power is primary.

results.title: Neoclouds Emerge as AI's Newest Infrastructure Bottleneck | Miami AI News
highlights:
Summary: Specialized cloud providers known as "neoclouds" are emerging to meet surging demand for AI computing power that traditional hyperscalers can't supply quickly enough. Companies such as CoreWeave, Lambda and Crusoe focus almost exclusively on renting high-performance Nvidia GPUs for AI training and inference. The model is attracting billions in investment while introducing new questions about financing, hardware depreciation and who ultimately controls access to AI's most valuable resource: compute.

The AI industry's biggest constraint isn't talent.

It isn't software.

It isn't even chips.

It's access to those chips.

That shortage has created one of the fastest-growing sectors in AI infrastructure: the rise of the "neocloud."

Unlike Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud, neocloud providers focus almost entirely on one business—leasing large clusters of Nvidia GPUs to companies building and deploying AI models.

As demand for computing power continues to outstrip supply, these specialist providers are becoming an increasingly important part of the AI ecosystem.

...

Their infrastructure is purpose-built for AI training and inference, allowing them to deploy GPU capacity quickly and efficiently for customers that need immediate access to high-performance computing.

...

Building GPU infrastructure is expensive.

Rather than relying solely on venture capital, many neocloud providers are financing expansion through debt, using Nvidia GPU assets as collateral.

That approach enables faster growth but also creates new financial risks.

If AI demand slows or newer chip generations quickly replace existing hardware, today's valuable GPU fleets could depreciate faster than lenders and investors expect.

It's a reminder that AI infrastructure isn't only a technology story—it's increasingly a capital markets story as well.

## A Business Built on Scarcity

The neocloud model depends on one central assumption: GPU demand will remain higher than available supply.

For now, that assumption appears well supported.

AI developers continue reporting long wait times for high-end GPU capacity, while enterprises deploying generative AI applications are placing growing pressure on cloud infrastructure.

As long as demand exceeds supply, specialist providers can command premium pricing and expand aggressively.

The challenge comes if the market eventually balances or new hardware significantly changes the economics of AI computing.

results.title: What Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron's capex mean for the ...
highlights:
With demand far outpacing supply, manufacturers are naturally resorting to expanding capacity.

However, there is a catch.

The industry in the spotlight has been burned before by such exuberance followed by expansion of manufacturing capacity, followed by oversupply, and then a crash.

Therefore, as once again billions are being committed in capex by these memory makers, investors are asking whether the industry is laying the groundwork for another painful memory chip oversupply cycle, as that would mean that the AI memory trade boom might be more short-lived than is being expected.

## AI demand has created an unprecedented supply crunch

Unlike previous technology cycles, the current AI wave has created an extraordinary imbalance between demand and supply.

According to TrendForce, data centres are expected to consume more than 70% of all high-end memory chips produced in 2026, leaving limited supply for traditional markets such as personal computers, smartphones and enterprise hardware.

HBM has become one of the most critical components inside AI servers because it enables processors to move enormous volumes of data at extremely high speeds, a requirement for training and running increasingly sophisticated AI models.

That shortage has allowed memory manufacturers to command premium pricing while posting record earnings.

However, history suggests that such periods rarely last indefinitely.

Over the past two decades, the memory industry has repeatedly followed the same pattern: demand surges, prices rise sharply, manufacturers rush to build new fabrication plants, production eventually floods the market, and prices collapse.

The most recent example came during 2022 and 2023, when Micron and SK Hynix suffered billions of dollars in losses after expanding production based on pandemic-era demand that faded far more quickly than expected.

For investors riding the lucrative AI memory trade, an unexpected pivot to oversupply risks compressing the explosive margins and premium valuations that chipmakers like SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung have enjoyed.

...

The industry's biggest risk remains the pace of AI infrastructure investment itself.

Memory stocks experienced sharp volatility throughout July as investors questioned whether hyperscale cloud providers were spending too aggressively on AI infrastructure.

The worry is that with the spend impacting balance sheets now, with lower reserves of cash, any potential pause in data centre building would mean the sky-high demand for memory and other semiconductor companies' products would suddenly drop.

Deloitte estimates that hyperscalers will devote roughly 30% of their data-centre capital expenditure to memory in 2026, rising to 36% in 2027.

"The current memory supply tightness and elevated prices may persist until 2029 or even 2030, assuming continued demand among hyperscalers for memory chips. Other customers that need memory for devices such as PCs, smartphones, and other consumer electronics, as well as for non-AI data centres, will likely also need to contend with high memory prices," Deloitte said.

Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya also believes concerns about a near-term downturn have become excessive.

Arya acknowledged that memory prices and profit margins are likely to normalize eventually as additional supply enters the market between mid-2027 and 2028.

However, he argued that the recent sell-off reflects investor positioning ahead of a potential downturn rather than any meaningful deterioration in demand.

"Hyperscaler spending continues to rise despite higher component costs, suggesting semis/memory pricing power," Arya wrote.

He noted that GPU rental rates remain near record highs and that no major cloud provider has indicated memory shortages are slowing AI deployments.

Following Micron's latest earnings, Bank of America extended its projected AI memory supercycle through the end of 2027, with a possible extension into 2030.

...

Arya said even under a bearish scenario in which DRAM

...

"We do not think the industry's underlying cyclicality has disappeared, but the mechanism behind it has changed. Long-term agreements now lock in pricing and allocation years in advance rather than quarter to quarter, giving buyers and sellers more visibility than in past cycles, when a shortage could reverse within a few quarters. That doesn't make memory a one-way trade — it makes the eventual turn slower to arrive, and potentially harder to time," Yip said.

results.title: Gavin Baker: Market Pullbacks Blur Accelerating AI Fundamentals and Compute Economics | AInformed
highlights:
Investor Gavin Baker argues that recent AI equity sell-offs misreflect real-world demand, as token growth, GPU rental spot prices, and hyperscaler cash flows continue to accelerate.

Despite a sharp market pull-back that sent many AI-related equities down 40% to 60% and brought Nvidia to its lowest forward price-to-earnings multiple in years, investor Gavin Baker contends that underlying market fundamentals are actually strengthening. Speaking on recent industry trends, Baker notes that key quantitative metrics tracked on the ground—including token generation growth, DRAM spot pricing, and GPU spot rental rates—show accelerating demand rather than deceleration. He points out that public market skepticism stems partly from a lack of visibility into private model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, alongside rapidly expanding open-source inference clouds.

A central component of Baker's thesis is that the market is misjudging how the next phase of the AI compute buildout will be financed. While widening credit default swaps and rising real yields have stoked fears of a risky debt-fueled capital cycle, operating cash flows for major hyperscalers including Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon accelerated significantly last quarter. Furthermore, as legacy long-term compute contracts roll off and reprice at higher current spot market rates, hyperscaler cash flows are poised to increase further. This dynamics could allow major technology firms to fund upcoming deployments of Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin chips largely through internal operating cash flow rather than relying heavily on debt.

Baker also reframes the rise of competitive open-source models, arguing that open-source adoption does not diminish overall hardware demand. Instead, open-source model usage shifts profit margins away from the proprietary frontier model layer and into the underlying cloud infrastructure layer. Because generating an open-source token requires the same computational flops, memory, and energy as a proprietary token, lower inference costs drive token elasticity, ultimately increasing total GPU compute hours consumed across the market.
